¶

'''17.''' Used in emphatic phrases expressing wonder, astonishment, perplexity, etc.: as, what in the ''world'' am I to do? how in all the ''world'' did you get there? — '''Above the world.''' See ''above.''— '''All the world.''' (''a'') Everybody.
{{smaller block|<poem>''All the wordle'' anon wenten hym again,
Men, wemen, children, of ech side moste and leste.</poem>
{{right|''Rom. of Partenay'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 48}}
<poem>’Tis the duke’s pleasure,
Whose disposition, ''all the world'' well knows,
Will not be rubb’d nor stopp’d.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Lear, ii. 2. 1}}}}
(''b'') The sum of what the world contains; everything: as, she is ''all the world'' to me. Compare ''the whole world'', below.
{{smaller block|<poem>For eni werk that he wrouȝt seththe i wol it hold,
ne wold i it were non other ''al the world'' to haue.</poem>
{{right|''William of Palerne'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 4}}}}
'''All the world and his wife,''' everybody; sometimes everybody worth speaking about; also, an ill-assorted mass. [Humorous.]
{{smaller block|''Miss'' ——. Pray, madam, who were the company?
''Lady Smart.'' Why, there was ''all the world and his wife.''
{{right|''Swift'', Polite Conversation,}}
''All the world and his wife'' and daughter leave cards.
{{right|''Dickens'', Our Mutual Friend, i.}}}}
'''All the world to a hand-saw†.''' See ''hand-saw.''— '''Archetypal world.''' See ''archetypal.''—'''A world,''' a great deal: used especially with a comparative force.
{{smaller block|<poem>’Tis ''a world'' to see,
How tame, when men and women are alone,
A meacock wretch can make the curstest shrew.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. of the S., ii. 1.}}
In the mills the boys are dressed in trousers ''a world'' too big, father’s or grandfather’s lopped off at the knees and all in tatters.
{{right|''The Century'', XLI.}}}}

''Secular'' and ''temporal'' are rarely used in a bad sense. ''Temporal'' is opposed to ''spiritual'' or ''eternal'': as, lords ''temporal''; merely ''temporal'' concerns. ''Earthly'' has, like ''worldly'', the sense of mundane, but in the sense of unspirituality it suggests more of grossness or groveling, a thought which is carried still further by ''earthy'', although ''earthy'' is not often used in that sense. '''worldly''' (wėrld′li), ''adv.'' [< ME. *''worldliche'', ''wordliche'', ''werdliche'', ''weoruldliche''; < ''worldly'', ''a.''] In a worldly manner; with relation to this life.
{{smaller block|<poem>Subverting ''worldly'' strong and ''worldly'' wise
By simply meek.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., xii. 568.}}}}

'''worldly-minded''' (wėrld′li-mīn″ded), ''a.'' Having a worldly mind; devoted to temporal pleasures and concerns.

'''worldly-mindedness''' (wėrld′li-mīn″ded-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being worldly-minded. ''Bp. Sanderson.''

'''worldly-wise''' (wėrld′li-wīz), ''a.'' Wise with reference to the affairs of this world.
{{smaller block|You then beheld things not as a ''worldly-wise'' man, but as a man of God.
{{right|''J. Bradford'', Letters (Parker Soc., 1853), II. 87.}}}}

'''world-old''' (wėrld′ōld), ''a.'' As old as the world; very old; reaching back through the ages.

'''world-riche†''', ''n.'' [ME., < ''world'' + ''riche''.] The kingdom of this world; the earth.
{{smaller block|<poem>For, as of trouthe, is ther noon her liche
Of al the women in this ''worlde-riche''.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Anelida and Arcite, l. 77.}}}}

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|world|6979|worm}}</noinclude>{{nop}}'''10.''' The part of mankind that is devoted to the affairs of this life or interested in secular affairs; those concerned especially for the interests and pleasures of the present state of existence; the unregenerate or ungodly part of humanity.
{{smaller block|I pray not for the ''world'', but for them which thou hast given me.
{{right|John xvii. 9.}}}}

'''11.''' The ways and manners of men; the practices of life; the habits, customs, and usages of society; social life in its various aspects.
{{smaller block|’Tis not good that children should know any wickedness; old folks, you know, have discretion, as they say, and know the ''world''.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. W. of W., ii. 2. 134.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The girl might pass, if we could get her
To know the ''world'' a little better.
(To know the ''world''! a modern phrase
For visits, ombre, balls, and plays).</poem>
{{right|''Swift'', Cadenus and Vanessa.}}}}
{{smaller block|Mr. Beauclerk was very entertaining this day, and told us a number of short stories in a lively, elegant manner, and with that air of the ''world'' which has I know not what impressive effect.
{{right|''Boswell'', Johnson, an. 1779.}}}}
{{smaller block|He had seen the ''world'', and mingled with society, yet retained the strong eccentricities of a man who had lived much alone.
{{right|''Irving.''}}}}

'''12.''' A course of life; a career.
{{smaller block|Persons of conscience will be afraid to begin the ''world'' unjustly.
{{right|''Richardson'', Clarissa Harlowe.}}}}

'''13.''' The current of events, especially as affecting the individual; circumstances or affairs, particularly those closely relating to one’s self.
{{smaller block|How goes the ''world'' with thee?
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., iii. 2. 98.}}}}

'''14.''' Any system of more or less complexity o development, characterized by harmony, orde or completeness; anything forming an organi whole; a microcosm.
{{smaller block|<poem>Man is one ''world'', and hath
Another to attend him.</poem>
{{right|''G. Herbert'', The Temple, Ma}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Dreams, books are each a ''world;'' and books, we know,
Are a substantial ''world'', both pure and good.</poem>
{{right|''Wordsworth'', Personal Tal}}}}

'''15.''' Sphere; domain; province; region; realn as, the ''world'' of dreams; the ''world'' of art.
{{smaller block|How it [moral philosophy] extendeth it selfe out of t limits of a mans own little ''world'' to the gouernment families, and maintayning of publique societies.
{{right|''Sir P. Sidney'', Apol. for Poetrie (ed. Arber), p. 3}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Will one beam be less intense,
When thy peculiar difference
Is cancell’d in the ''world'' of sense?</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Two Voic}}}}

'''16.''' A great number or quantity: as, a ''wor'' of people; a ''world'' of words; a ''world'' of mea ing. Compare ''a world'', below.
{{smaller block|<poem>He holt aboute him alwey, out of drede,
A ''world'' of folk, as com him wel of kynde,
The fressheste and the beste he koude fynde.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, iii. 17}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I can go no where
Without a ''world'' of offerings to my excellence.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Humorous Lieutenant, iv.}}}}
{{smaller block|There must a ''world'' of ceremonies pass.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Alchemist, i.}}}}
{{smaller block|Being lead through the Synagogue into a privat hou I found a ''world'' of people in a chamber.
{{right|''Evelyn'', Diary, Jan. 15, 16}}}}
{{smaller block|It cost me a ''world'' of woe.
{{right|''Tennyson'', The Grandmoth}}}}

'''Axis of the world.''' See ''axis''<sup>1</sup>.—'''Ectypal world.''' See ''ectypal.''—'''External world.''' See ''external.''—'''For all the world,''' from every point of view; exactly; precisely; entirely.
{{smaller block|<poem>''For al the world'' swiche a wolf as we here seiȝen,
It semeth riȝt that selue bi semblant & bi hewe.</poem>
{{right|''William of Palerne'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 3501.}}}}
{{smaller block|He was, ''for all the world,'' like a forked radish.
{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. IV., iii. 2. 334.}}}}
'''Man of the world.''' See ''man.''—'''Noëtic world.''' See ''noëtic.''—'''Prince of this world.''' See ''prince.''—'''The New World.''' See ''new.''—'''The Old World,''' the eastern hemisphere, comprising Europe, Asia, and Africa: so called from being that in which civilization first arose.—'''The other world.''' See ''other''<sup>1</sup>.—'''The whole world,''' the sum of what the world contains; the representative or equivalent of all worldly possessions: as, to gain ''the whole world.''—'''The world’s end,''' the remotest part of the earth; the most distant regions.—'''To carry the world before one.''' See ''carry.''—'''To go to the world†,''' to get married.
{{smaller block|Thus ''goes'' every one ''to the world'' but I; . . . I may sit in a corner and cry heigh-ho for a husband.
{{right|''Shak.'', Much Ado, ii. 1. 331.}}}}
{{smaller block|Hence the expression ''woman of the world'' (that is, a married woman), used by Audrey in “As you Like it.”
I hope it is no dishonest desire to desire to be a ''woman of the world.'' {{right|''Shak.'', As you Like it, v. 3. 5.}}}}
'''To make a noise in the world.''' See ''noise.''—'''Woman of the world.''' See ''woman.'' See also ''to go to the world,'' above.—'''World without end,''' to all eternity; eternally; unceasingly: also used attributively, meaning ‘never-ending,’ as in the quotation from Shakspere.
{{smaller block|<poem>Nor dare I chide the ''world-without-end'' hour,
Whilst I, my sovereign, watch the clock for you.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Sonnets, lvii.}}}}
{{smaller block|This man . . . thinks by talking ''world without end'' to make good his integrity. {{right|''Milton.''}}}}

{{smaller|=Syn. '''5.''' ''Globe'', etc. See ''earth''<sup>1</sup>.}}

'''world†''' (wėrld), ''v. t.''   [< ''world'', ''n.'']   To introduce into the world; give birth to.
{{smaller block|Like Lightening, it can strike the Child in the womb, and kill it ere ’tis ''worlded'', when the Mother shall remain unhurt.
{{right|''Feltham'', Resolves, i. 59.}}}}

'''worlded''' (wėr′ded), ''a.'' Containing worlds. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>The fires that arch this dusky dot—
Yon myriad-''worlded'' way.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Epilogue.}}}}

'''world-hardened''' (wėrld′här″dnd), ''a.'' Hardened by the love of worldly things.

'''worldhood†''' (wėrld′hu̇d), ''n.''   [< ''world'' + ''-hood''.]   A worldly possession. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Content yourselves with what you have already, or else seek honest means whereby to increase your ''worldhoods''.
{{right|''Henry VIII. of Eng.'', quoted in I. D’Israeli’s Amen. of [Lit., I. 363.}}}}

'''world-language''' (wėrld′lang″gwāj), ''n.'' A language used by or known to the civilized world.
{{smaller block|Jericzek was already well versed in the two classical and four great modern ''world-languages''.
{{right|''Athenæum'', No. 3226, p. 256.}}}}

'''worldliness''' (wėrld′li-nes), ''n.''   [< ME. ''werldlinesse'', ''werdlinesse''; < ''worldly'' + ''-ness''.]   The state or character of being worldly; worldly conduct. ''Jer. Taylor.''
{{smaller block|You may call your way of thinking prudence. I call it sinful ''worldliness''.
{{right|''Thackeray'', Philip, xviii.}}}}

'''worldling''' (wėrld′ling), ''n.''   [< ''world'' + ''-ling''<sup>1</sup>.]   One who is worldly; one devoted to the affairs and interests of this life.
{{smaller block|A foutre for the world and ''worldlings'' base!
{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. IV., v. 3. 103.}}}}
<poem>''Worldlings'', whose whimp’ring folly holds the losses
Of honor, pleasure, health, and wealth such crosses.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Quarles'', Emblems, i., Epig. 6.}}}}

'''worldly''' (wėrld′li), ''a.''   [< ME. ''worldly'', ''worldlich'', ''wurldlic'', ''weoreldlike'', < AS. ''weoruldlic''; as ''world'' + ''-ly''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' Of or pertaining to the world or the present state of existence; temporal; earthly.
{{smaller block|With all my ''worldly'' goods I thee endow.
{{right|''Book of Common Prayer'', Solemnization of Matrimony.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Repose you here in rest,
Secure from ''worldly'' chances and mishaps!</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Tit. And., i. 1. 152.}}}}
'''2.''' Secular: opposed to ''monastic.''
{{smaller block|<poem>May men fynde religioun
In ''worldly'' habitacioun.</poem>
{{right|''Rom. of the Rose'', l. 6226.}}}}
'''3.''' Devoted to, interested in, or connected with this present life, and its cares, advantages, or pleasures, to the exclusion of those of a future life; desirous of temporal benefit or enjoyment merely; earthly, as opposed to ''heavenly'' or ''spiritual;'' carnal; sordid; vile: as, ''worldly'' lusts, cares, affections, pleasures; ''worldly'' men.
{{smaller block|<poem>To live secure,
''Worldly'' or dissolute. ''Milton'', P. L., xi. 803.</poem>
Interest, pride, and ''worldly'' honour. ''Dryden.'' (''Johnson.'')}}
{{smaller|='''Syn. 1.''' Mundane, terrestrial, sublunary.—'''1''' and '''3.''' ''Worldly'', ''Secular'', ''Temporal'', ''Earthly'', ''Earthy'', ''Unspiritual'', ''Carnal.'' ''Worldly'' means of the world, in fact or in spirit, in distinction from that which is above the world; as applying to mind, it indicates a pleasure in the things that belong to the external life and a disregard of spiritual or even intellectual pleasures: it is opposed to ''spiritual'', expressing positively what ''unspiritual'' expresses negatively. ''Secular'' is opposed to ''sacred'' or to ''ecclesiastical'': as, there are six ''secular'' days in the week; the ''secular'' arm. ''Secular'' and ''temporal'' are rarely used in a bad sense. ''Temporal'' is opposed to ''spiritual'' or ''eternal'': as, lords ''temporal''; merely ''temporal'' concerns. ''Earthly'' has, like ''worldly'', the sense of mundane, but in the sense of unspirituality it suggests more of grossness or groveling, a thought which is carried still further by ''earthy'', although ''earthy'' is not often used in that sense. ''Carnal'' suggests that which belongs to the gratification of the animal nature; it ranges from the merely unspiritual to the sensual. See ''sensual'' and ''temporal''.}}

{{smaller block|<poem>Subverting ''worldly'' strong and ''worldly'' wise
By simply meek.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., xii. 568.}}}}

'''worldly-minded''' (wėrld′li-mīn″ded), ''a.'' Having a worldly mind; devoted to temporal pleasures and concerns.

'''worldly-mindedness''' (wėrld′li-mīn″ded-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being worldly-minded. ''Bp. Sanderson.''

'''worldly-wise''' (wėrld′li-wīz), ''a.'' Wise with reference to the affairs of this world.
{{smaller block|You then beheld things not as a ''worldly-wise'' man, but as a man of God.
{{right|''J. Bradford'', Letters (Parker Soc., 1853), II. 87.}}}}

'''world-old''' (wėrld′ōld), ''a.'' As old as the world; very old; reaching back through the ages.

'''world-riche†''', ''n.''   [ME., < ''world'' + ''riche''.]   The kingdom of this world; the earth.
{{smaller block|<poem>For, as of trouthe, is ther noon her liche
Of al the women in this ''worlde-riche''.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Anelida and Arcite, l. 77.}}}}

'''world-wearied''' (wėrld′wēr″id), ''a.'' Tired of the world.

'''world-wide''' (wėrld′wīd), ''a.'' As wide as the world; extending over or pervading all the world; widely spread: as, ''world-wide'' fame; specifically, in ''zoögeog.'', cosmopolitan: noting such habitat, or the fact of such distribution, but not the species or individuals themselves which inhabit all parts of the world.

'''worm''' (wėrm), ''n.''   [< ME. ''worm'', ''wurm'', ''wirm'', ''werm'', < AS. ''wyrm'', a worm, snake, dragon, = OS. ''wurm'' = D. LG. ''worm'' = OHG. MHG. G. ''wurm'', worm, insect, snake, dragon, = Icel. ''ormr'' (for *''vormr'') = Sw. Dan. ''orm'' (for *''vorm'') = Goth. ''waurms'', a worm, = L. ''vermis''; cf. Gr. ῥόμος, ῥόμοξ (*Ϝρόμος), a wood-worm; cf. Lith. ''kirmis'', worm, = OBulg. ''chrŭvĭ'' = Russ. ''chervŭ'', worm, = OIr. ''cruim'', a worm (cf. Ir. ''cruimh'', a maggot, W. ''pryf'', worm), = Skt. ''krimi'', worm (whence ult. E. ''crimson'', ''carmine'', q. v.). From the L. ''vermis'' are ult. E. ''vermin'', ''vermicule'', ''vermeil'', etc.]   '''1.''' In popular language, any small creeping creature whose body consists of a number of movable joints or rings, and whose limbs are very short or entirely wanting; any vermiform animal.
{{smaller block|<poem>Nowe pike oute mougthes, attercoppes, ''wormys'',
And butterflie whoos thoste engendryng ''worme'' is.</poem>
{{right|''Palladius'', Husbondrie (E. E. T. S.), p. 138.}}}}
{{smaller block|(''a'') Any annelid, as the earthworm, lobworm or lugworm, leech, etc. See the distinctive names.}}
{{smaller block|''Worms'' have played a more important part in the history of the world than most persons would at first suppose. In almost all humid countries they are extraordinarily numerous, and for their size possess great muscular power.
{{right|''Darwin'', Vegetable Mould, p. 305.}}}} (''b'') Any helminth, whether parasitic or not, as a flatworm, brain-worm, fluke-worm, roundworm, tapeworm, pinworm, hairworm, threadworm, spoonworm, longworm, whirl-worm, guinea-worm, etc. See such words, and ''vinegar-eel.'' (''c'') One of several long slender vermiform echinoderms, as some holothurians and related forms. See ''Vermiformia,'' and cuts under ''Synapta'' and ''trepang.'' (''d'') Some small or slender acarine or mite, or its larva, as the worm found in sebaceous follicles. See ''comedo'' and ''Demodex.'' (''e'') A myriapod; a centiped or milleped; a gally-worm. (''f'') The larva, grub, maggot, or caterpillar of many true hexapod insects: as, bag-''worm''; boll-''worm''; book-''worm''; wire-''worm''; sod-''worm''; snake-''worm''; joint-''worm''; silk''worms.'' See the compounded and otherwise qualified names.
{{smaller block|The larvæ of the bee-moth are frequently but improperly so called. Indeed when ''worms'' are spoken of by the ordinary beekeeper, the larvæ of the bee-moth are almost always meant.
{{right|''Phin'', Dict. Apiculture, p. 78.}}}}
(''g'') The adult of some true insects whose body is long and flexible, as a glow-worm. (''h'') One of several long slender crustaceans with short legs or none, which attach to or burrow in other animals, bore into wood, etc., as some kinds of fish-lice, certain isopods (as the gribble), certain amphipods (as the wood-shrimp), etc. (''i'') One of some vermiform mollusks, as a teredo or shipworm, or a worm-shell. See cuts under ''shipworm'' and ''Vermetus.'' (''j'') A small lizard with rudimentary legs, or none, as a blind-worm or slow-worm. (''k''†) A serpent; a snake; a dragon. For a modern instance in composition, see ''worm-snake'', 1.
{{smaller block|<poem>He [Satan] . . .
Wente in to a ''wirme'', and tolde eue a tale.</poem>
{{right|''Genesis and Exodus'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 321.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Hast thou the pretty ''worm'' of Nilus there,
That kills and pains not?</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', A. and C., v. 2. 243.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Here will be subject for my snakes and me.
Cling to my neck and wrists, my loving ''worms.''</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Poetaster, Ind.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
